summary:
The Maldives criminalises same-sex conduct and same-sex marriage under its Penal Code, whose amended provisions took effect in 2015. Section 131 defines criminal sexual contact as sexual contact without a reason permitted under Islamic law, and section 411(2) names same-sex intercourse as an offence under section 411(f). Section 410(a)(8), in force since 16 July 2015, criminalises marriage between two persons of the same sex. Penalties run to one year for unlawful marriage under section 410(a)(8), up to eight years for the conduct covered by sections 411(a)(2) and 411(d), with a supplementary 100 lashes available under Sharia, and up to four years for unlawful sexual conduct under section 412. The 2014 code extended the offence beyond Muslims to all persons.

Reporting in 2015 described death-penalty provisions as theoretically in reach for the offence. The statute's own terms are narrower: sections 92(k) and 1205 make death available only for egregious purposeful killing, capital punishment has been suspended since 1953, and plans to resume executions were later abandoned.

No transgender-specific criminal provision, document rule, screening procedure, facility rule, custody rule or care rule has been identified. Codified offences and penalties concern same-sex sexual activity and same-sex marriage. There is no legal protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity, and none on grounds of sexual orientation.

Enforcement is documented. Police on Dhaandhoo arrested two men, aged 56 and 27, on 29 August 2015 after a public complaint about homosexual activity in their private home. The prosecution reached into a residence on a local island, so exposure is not confined to public space or to Maldivian nationals. Rainbow Warriors warned after the arrests that tourists could face similar threats. Prosecutions are rare, but homosexuality remains a social taboo.

Tourist infrastructure operates at a distance from the criminal regime. Private tourist islands, resorts and hotels are usually isolated from civilian population centres and are not subject to Islamic law, as the sale of alcohol there indicates. LGBTQ tourists are generally considered welcome at these properties, and LGBTQ couples visiting resorts rarely encounter the Islamic-based law that applies elsewhere. Guides advise caution over public displays of affection outside tourist areas. Anti-LGBTQ discrimination is pervasive in the country as a whole.

The Maldives holds reservations to the ICCPR, CEDAW and the CRC. In review by the UN Human Rights Committee, the government was recommended to adopt anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and to act against the stigmatisation of homosexuals. The United Nations Population Fund reported that people perceived as homosexual or transgender were the target of hate crimes and other human rights violations and recommended law reform to protect them; the Maldives noted those recommendations without accepting them. The government rejected 60 Universal Periodic Review recommendations, including matters said to contradict the Islamic faith and the Constitution, among them recommendations on lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and non-traditional forms of the family. The Maldives signed the 2008 statement opposing decriminalisation and rejected UN resolutions on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2011 and September 2014.

A 2024 expert survey by the Human Rights Measurement Initiative found LGBTQIA+ people among the groups most commonly identified by human-rights experts as at risk of empowerment-rights violations, alongside migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers. Political participation scored relatively better at 6.4 out of 10, while other civil and political rights scored considerably lower.

Violence against LGBT people is documented. Gay blogger Hilath Rasheed was stabbed in the neck in Malé in 2013. In 2014 a gay Maldivian, Abraham Naim, was granted asylum in New Zealand on the basis that he was at risk of serious harm from state agents; a President's Office spokesman said that people seeking asylum on grounds of sexual-orientation discrimination would face prosecution on return. A 2020 United States country report found no reports of officials complicit in abuses against LGBTI persons, while noting that societal stigma likely discouraged reporting.
tangentialFactors:
In its own submission to the 2015 Universal Periodic Review, the government reported that of 126 first-cycle recommendations it fully accepted 89, partially accepted 11, took note of 6 and rejected 20 with reasons, and that over four years it had fully implemented 58 and partially implemented 32.

The Maldives' reservations to the ICCPR, CEDAW and the CRC sit alongside concerns recorded in the March 2015 OHCHR compilation about sharia-based treatment of children born outside marriage.
localsOnly:
Rainbow Warriors describes the Maldivian LGBTQ movement as mostly limited to the virtual world, operating on the internet because of the intensity of homophobia in the country.

Local citizens who express support for LGBTI rights on social media are targeted for online harassment and labelled apostates or irreligious, according to a 2020 United States country report.

Societal stigma likely discourages reporting of abuses against LGBTI people, the same report found, and no officials were reported complicit in such abuses.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents societal tolerance or hostility toward transgender people as a distinct group; the descriptions of tolerance and of hostility concern LGBTQ people generally, homosexuality, or homophobia.

No transgender-specific document, marker, screening, facility, custody or care rule is recorded, and no data on how trans travellers are processed at entry or in custody was identified.

Enforcement evidence is limited to a single documented 2015 prosecution on a local island; the frequency of prosecutions, and whether tourists have been charged, is not established by the sources.

Sources disagree on the death penalty's availability for same-sex conduct: 2015 reporting described it as theoretically in reach, while the statute reserves capital punishment for egregious purposeful killing and executions have been suspended since 1953.
